text: Okay, I've heard you all. Okay, my take on the issue. The politics that has exploded over Sonam Wangchuk's fast and students' protests should come as no surprise. With the Parliament session due next week, the political battle lines are clearly being drawn. But beyond the polarized politics, there is a larger issue of how to deal with such protests. From Anna Hazare to Sonam Wangchuk, India has a proud tradition of peaceful Gandhian protests. Governments need not agree with every demand of the protesters, but they weaken democracy if they respond with silence, excessive force, or treating dissenters as simply a law and order problem. Student movements and citizen movements have often been catalysts for democratic change in this country. A nation that has celebrated dissent in the past cannot criminalize or ignore it in the present. Resignation of any minister may not resolve the issue of poorly conducted exams But surely ignoring the genuine concerns of many of the protests raises the larger question of democratic accountability that simply cannot be brushed aside so easily. Think about it.
